## Paper

## Abstract

The distinction between vacuum-field and source-radiation effects in phenomena such as the Lamb shift, Casimir forces, and spontaneous emission relies on additional assumptions at the theoretical level, and an experimental approach was never considered feasible. Fermi’s two-atom problem, a Gedankenexperiment on how atoms interact with the electromagnetic field via vacuum and source radiation, provides key theoretical insight. Advances in ultrafast optics now enable experimental analogues using two laser pulses in a nonlinear crystal. Here we demonstrate the detection of vacuum- and source-radiation-induced correlations between two pulses, separated by their causal properties. Specifically, vacuum fluctuations and source radiation are shown to correlate distinct quadratures of near-infrared pulses, enabling individual probing via phase-sensitive detection. Our results experimentally verify the time-domain fluctuation-dissipation theorem at the quantum level and open avenues for studying quantum radiation effects in time-dependent media, including entanglement harvesting from the vacuum and quantum field detection in curved-space analogues.

---

## Introduction

Fermi’s two-atom setup consists of two atoms in empty space whose interaction with the vacuum radiation field is abruptly switched on. Studying the subsequent build-up of correlations between the atoms reveals fundamental properties of quantum fields in space and time1–4.

In the Heisenberg picture, independent of the initial state of the two atoms, two different terms contribute to these correlations5–8, as illustrated in Fig. 1a. On the one hand, correlations between the two atoms arise from their individual interaction with the ground-state electromagnetic field—the vacuum fluctuations—whereby correlations intrinsically existing in the vacuum field are swapped to the atoms1–4. On the other hand, the two atoms can exchange a photon. The emission of this photon is triggered by the interaction of one atom with its own radiative field (radiation reaction). This radiation is known as source radiation1,6 and interacts with the other atom, which leads to correlations between the atoms. Mathematically, individual contributions of vacuum fluctuations and source radiation to fundamental processes in quantum electrodynamics, such as spontaneous emission or the Lamb shift, are in general not uniquely determined, since they depend on the initial ordering of the atomic and field operators in the light-matter interaction Hamiltonian6,9,10.

While for most of the phenomena associated with interactions with the ground state of light, vacuum fluctuations and source radiation can therefore be seen as inseparable “two sides of the same quantum mechanical coin”10, they have a different character regarding causality in Fermi’s two-atom problem: The vacuum-induced correlations arise instantaneously upon turning on the interaction, while the exchange of a photon leads to correlations only after the propagation time δt=r/c7,8. However, different choices of the aforementioned operator ordering can lead to a non-causal description of source radiation, making its interpretation ambiguous7. This issue remains purely theoretical unless the two contributions can be observed independently. Yet, an experimental investigation has long been considered unfeasible due to the challenge of initiating the two atoms, rapidly switching their interaction with the field on ultra-short timescales, and detecting the resulting correlations11. Here, we overcome these limitations using an all-optical version of Fermi’s two-atom setup and probe the contributions from source radiation and vacuum field fluctuations, separated by causality, individually for the first time.

In contrast to atoms, the interaction of laser pulses with a surrounding electromagnetic field can be initiated and terminated on ultrashort timescales as the pulses enter and leave a nonlinear material. This unique property has enabled an all-optical analog of Fermi’s two-atom setup, where vacuum-induced correlations between atoms are mapped onto two spatially separated laser pulses interacting with the vacuum field inside a nonlinear crystal12 (see Fig. 1b). The implementation relies on electro-optic sampling, in which near-infrared probe pulses couple to a terahertz or mid-infrared field (possibly in the vacuum state and restricted to the spectral width of the probe), generating a second-order nonlinear field polarized perpendicular to the probe13–15. This nonlinear interaction modifies the polarization state of the two probe pulses, directly paralleling the transition of the atoms in the Fermi setup. Here, however, the resonant single-mode transition of two-level atoms is replaced by an off-resonant, broadband coupling of multimode near-infrared pulses to terahertz field modes within the spectral width of the probes. The use of femtosecond pulses thus not only allows the interaction to be switched on and off with high temporal precision, but also enables the application of advanced quantum optics detection techniques to analyze the polarization state of the probes (see refs. 7, 12, 16 and Supplementary Information Note 1.A for further comparison between Fermi’s two-atom setup and two-beam electro-optic sampling).

Recently, an experiment similar to the one in ref. 12 has been theoretically suggested7, which would be capable of individually detecting correlations caused by source radiation as well (see Fig. 1c), and in the following, we demonstrate its experimental implementation.

---

## Results

The idea relies on the fact that in the electro-optic sampling analog of Fermi’s two-atom setup, vacuum-field fluctuations (given by the correlation function of the THz vacuum field C(r,r',t,t')=1/2h[Eb(r,t),Eb(r',t')]i) and source radiation (given by the response function R(r,r',t,t')=(i/ℏ)θ(t-t')h[Eb(r,t),Eb(r',t')]i) correlate different quadratures of the two near-infrared pulses, which allows one to individually probe them by changing the phase plate in the employed homodyne detection scheme (see Fig. 1b, c). This distinction mirrors the situation in Fermi’s two-atom problem, where different Pauli matrices are correlated depending on whether the correlation originates from vacuum fluctuations or from source radiation7.

In the vacuum-field contribution, the near-infrared field of the two pulses individually interacts with the vacuum field at terahertz frequencies. Due to the retardance of π/2 occurring in the non-linear process, the generated field that contains the information about the THz field is out-of-phase with the probe field. As a consequence, correlations induced by terahertz vacuum fluctuations can be detected through quarter-wave plates in the homodyne detection schemes of both probe beams, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 1b. The instantaneous correlation of the two pulses induced by the terahertz vacuum fluctuations is obtained from the individually detected signals as a function of different time delays between the two probe pulses12. In the source radiation contribution schematically depicted in Fig. 1c, the electric field of one probe pulse interacts with the copropagating ground-state fluctuations in the near-infrared, resulting in the emission of source radiation. The second pulse then interacts with that terahertz source radiation in the same way as with the terahertz vacuum field again leading to a nonlinear field contribution that has a quadrature out-of-phase with the probe field. In contrast, to trigger the source radiation, the probe field of the first pulse interacted with the in-phase quadrature of the near-infrared vacuum fluctuations. To observe the correlations resulting from source radiation, one thus has to probe the first pulse with a half-wave plate—thereby accessing the quadrature that is in-phase with the pulse—and the second with a quarter-wave plate as in the vacuum field contribution (see ref. 7 for details and Supplementary Information Note 1.B).

For the experimental realization, a similar optical setup as in ref. 12 is utilized and schematically shown in Fig. 2a. To compensate for dispersion and obtain 110 fs-short pulses inside the detection crystal, the probe signal is pre-stretched in a prism compressor before being separated into the two individual probe signals (see the “Methods” section about experimental setup and Supplementary Information Note 2.D). The correlations between different quadratures of the field amplitudes of the two laser pulses emerging from the crystal are detected by probing the correlations between two sets of balanced detectors, each of which has a tunable waveplate determining the probed quadrature (see Fig. 1b, c and the “Methods” section). In agreement with ref. 12, the vacuum-induced correlation measured with two beams at a target distance of 50 μm and with a quarter-wave plate on both detection lines oscillates symmetrically around zero time delay δt with the maximum correlation for δt=0 (blue line in Fig. 2b). Compared to previous results, the reduced pulse duration increases the observed peak correlation to more than 5 V2/m212,15.

For the setup sensitive to correlations stemming from source radiation (combination of a half-wave plate on one and a quarter-wave plate on the other detection line), the temporal correlation (green line in Fig. 1b) is asymmetric. Confirming the causal nature of the correlations induced by source radiation, the signal occurs mainly for positive time delays δt > 0, while the residual correlations δt ≲ 0 arise from the finite spatio-temporal Gaussian extension of the laser pulses12.

The Fourier transform of the correlation traces for vacuum fluctuations and source radiation are plotted in Fig. 2c. Compared to our previous results, the signal bandwidth now extends to 4.5 THz due to the shorter pulse length12. The initial increase in the signal with frequency up to 2 THz is due to the increasing strength of the vacuum fluctuations with frequency. Above 2.5 THz, the two signals change sign as the distance between the two beams becomes comparable to the wavelength inside the crystal. The slight shift of the zero crossing of the experimentally observed vacuum-induced correlation compared to the theoretical model might be caused by a slight shift of the beam distance towards 30 μm for the measurement in a configuration sensitive to vacuum fluctuations (details in the Supplementary Information Note 2.C).

The vacuum field and source radiation signals are further not independent from each other but connected via the fluctuation-dissipation theorem in the quantum limit (zero temperature). It predicts a connection between the correlation that stems from vacuum fluctuations and source radiation in the time domain through the Hilbert transform, which is validated in the experimental data in Fig. 2b through the phase shift of π/2 between the two correlations7,17. In the frequency domain, this leads to a direct relation between the real part of the vacuum-induced correlation (blue solid line) and the imaginary part of the correlation caused by source radiation (green solid line), which are plotted in Fig. 2c. Theoretic calculations (plotted in dashed lines) predict that the imaginary part of the source radiation signal is equivalent to the vacuum-induced correlations multiplied by a factor of -1/27. When comparing the experimentally observed correlations, the imaginary part of the correlation caused by source radiation (green line) matches well the expectation based on the vacuum-induced correlation (gray line). The slight deviation between those two curves and between the experimental and theoretical data is mainly caused by the distance between the two beams inside the crystal, which deviated from the target value of 50 μm and between the two measurements (details in the Supplementary Information Note II.C).

---

## Methods

Experimental setup
The optical setup to detect electro-optic correlations is shown schematically in Fig. 2a of the main text. We are using the pulsed signal of a Ti:sapphire laser. To compensate for the dispersion of the transmission optics, we implemented a prism compressor. The beam position is actively stabilized to reduce long-term drifts. A beam splitter divides the intensity of the pulse into two individual probe signals. The delay stage controls the time delay δt between the two beams. The two beams are placed in close proximity to each other, and two piezo-controlled mirrors set the angle between the two beams. Afterwards, the two beams are directed inside a dilution fridge.

Inside the cryostat, a 50 mm lens focuses the beams into a 〈110〉-cut zinc-telluride crystal. The angle of the two beams determines the distance of the two beams in the focal plane and is adjusted to a distance of 50 μm in the current experiment. Since the beam waist measures 10 μm, the two beams are well-separated inside the nonlinear crystal. A second lens re-collimates the beams afterwards. Both lenses and the nonlinear crystal are thermally connected to the 4 K-plate of the cryostat to suppress thermal radiation in the terahertz regime. The two beams are propagating along the 〈110〉-axis of the zinc telluride and are polarized along the 〈001〉-direction.

After leaving the cryostat, the two probe beams are separated, and the change in polarization is analyzed individually using the combination of a wave plate, a polarizing beam splitter, and a balanced detector. The correlation of the two signals is calculated for each individual pulse pair using a fast acquisition card. Further details about the setup and data acquisition, which is suppressing slowly varying correlations, are reported in ref. 15.

Experimentally observed correlation
In general, the signal observed in electro-optic sampling can be expressed in terms of a difference in photon-number S=Nperp - Npara of the two outputs of the polarizing beam splitter (perpendicular Nperp and parallel Npara polarized) measured by the balanced detector13. For a wave plate with arbitrary retardance γ, the signal is given by:

Sγ=4πϵ0c/ℏ ∫ dω P(γ) Ebx(r?,ω)Ebz(r?,ω) + H.c., (1)

where Ebz(r?,ω) denotes the NIR field at the end face of the detection crystal polarized along the crystallographic 〈001〉-axis and is given by the field of the probe signal, and Ebx(r?,ω) is the field along the 〈110〉, which is determined by the NIR vacuum fluctuations and the nonlinear field induced by the THz vacuum field and the source radiation. The influence of the wave-plate retardance γ is described by the following function:

P(γ) = -cos(γ) - 2i cos(γ/2) / 2. (2)

Within the experiment, we measure two electro-optic signals, Stγ(0) and Sτγ(δt), where δt denotes the delay between the two probe pulses. For vacuum fluctuations, both detection schemes employ a quarter-wave plate (γt=γτ=π/2), and the experimentally observed correlation is given by:

G(1)VF(δt) = h0|Stπ/2(0), Sτπ/2(δt)|0i. (3)

For source radiation, the detection configuration consists of a half-wave plate for the first probe (γt=π) and a quarter-wave plate for the second (γτ=π/2), yielding

G(1)SR(δt) = h0|Stπ(0), Sτπ/2(δt)|0i. (4)

Here, Nt and Nτ denote the total number of detected photons in the two probe signals and the refractive index n=2.85 at frequency ωp=2π×375 THz, the electro-optic coefficient of zinc telluride r41=3.9 pm V−1, the speed of light c, and the length of the detection crystal l=1 mm, and converts the unitless correlation of photon numbers into a field correlation as presented in Fig. 2.

Theoretical model
To model the experiments, we use the theoretical framework of two-beam electro-optical sampling developed in ref. 7. It builds on previous works in refs. 13, 26.

Applying the paraxial wave-approximation to all involved near-infrared fields but not the THz field26, the electro-optic sampling signal with two quarter-wave plates reads7

G(δt) = ∫ d3r dt d3r0 dt0 L(r,t)L(r0,t0) C(r,r0,t,t0). (5)

With a quarter-wave plate for pulse one and a half-wave plate for pulse two it is in turn given by:

G(δt) = -ℏ ∫ d3r dt d3r0 dt0 L(r,t)L(r0,t0) R(r,r0,t,t0). (6)

Here, V is the volume of the nonlinear crystal and L(r,t)=L(r-δre x,t-δt)=(2/π)3/2 e-2(t-ngz/c)2/τ2 σ e-2r2/w2 [r∥=(rx,rz), w: beam waist, τσ: pulse duration, ng: group refractive index in the near-infrared] are the Gaussian-shaped pulse envelopes of the two laser pulses. The response and correlation functions of the x-polarized THz field Eb(r,t) inside the crystal accounting for dispersion and absorption are defined in the main text and can be evaluated using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics27. In frequency domain, they are given by R(r,r0,Ω)=μ0Ω2D(r,r0,Ω)/(2π) and C(r,r0,Ω)=ℏμ0sgn[Ω]Ω2Im[D(r,r0,Ω)]/(2π), respectively, with the xx component of the dyadic Green tensor of the vector Helmholtz equation D and the vacuum permeability μ0.

We further follow ref. 7 to numerically evaluate Eqs. (5) and (6). The resulting frequency domain correlation signals defined by G(Ω)=(1/2π) ∫ dδt G(δt) eiΩδt are shown in Fig. 2c. We used the following parameters in the simulation, which, except for ng, have all been independently determined experimentally: pulse duration τ=110 fs, Gaussian beam width w=10 μm, beam separation δr=50 μm, and the group refractive index in the near-infrared ng=3.18. The refractive index in the THz is given by:

n(Ω) = sqrt(ϵ∞ + (ℏωLO)2 - (ℏωTO)2 / (ℏωTO)2 - (ℏΩ)2 - iℏΩγ), (7)

with all parameters as measured in ref. 28 for a ZnTe crystal at temperature T=300 K, except that we use ϵ∞=7.38 to match the real part of the refractive index measured at T=4 K reported in ref. 12.

Note that the influence of the phonon resonance at 5.3 THz starts to increase above 4 THz, which in turn leads to an enhancement of the local (longitudinal) field fluctuations26, but also to an increase in absorption. As a result of the absorption and the longitudinal nature of these fluctuations, the spatial range of correlations in the quantum vacuum as well as the propagation of source radiation from one beam to the other are delimited, and the detected electro-optic correlation in Fig. 2c vanishes in that frequency range. This means that the bandwidth of our detection is actually not limited by the bandwidth of the laser pulse but by the onset of increasing losses due to the phonon resonance above ≈4 THz, and makes it crucial that our theoretical framework accounts for absorption via a complex permittivity.

The fluctuation dissipation theorem implies C(r,r0,Ω)=ℏsgn(Ω)Im[R(r,r0,Ω)], leading to the relation between G(Ω) and G(Ω) discussed in the main text7.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

Quantum electrodynamics effects such as spontaneous emission, Lamb shift, and Casimir-Polder forces can be attributed to
vacuum fluctuations, source reaction, or a combination of both. Theoretically, this ambiguity was settled by Dalibard,
Dupont-Roc, and Cohen-Tannoudji, who proposed that the symmetric operator ordering between the variables of the atoms
and the field should be adopted in order to ensure that the effective Hamiltonians originating from vacuum fluctuations and
radiation reaction are separately Hermitian. However, it was generally believed that only the total effect is experimentally
observable, and not the individual contributions. In this work, the authors propose a method to experimentally distinguish
these two contributions. Based on recent advances in ultrafast optics, they present an optical analog of Fermi’s two-atom
problem using two laser pulses propagating through a nonlinear crystal. Through phase-sensitive detection, they
demonstrate that vacuum fluctuations and source radiation correlate different quadratures of the laser pulses, allowing for
their individual detection. This approach also provides an experimental verification of the time-domain fluctuation-dissipation
theorem at the quantum level. Before recommending the paper for publication in Nature Communications, I have the
following questions and comments.
1. In the abstract, the authors wrote: “The unique distinction between vacuum-field and source-radiation induced effects in
processes such as the Lamb shift, Casimir forces or spontaneous emission, remains unresolved even at the theoretical
level, and an experimental approach was never considered feasible” and “Beyond resolving a longstanding theoretical
ambiguity”. While I agree that experimentally separating these two contributions was long considered unfeasible, it should
be noted that, theoretically, this ambiguity has been solved by Dalibard, Dupont-Roc, and Cohen-Tannoudji in the 1980s.
2. In Line 41, the authors wrote: ”On the other hand, the two atoms can exchange a real photon.” It would be clearer to
specify the initial state of the atoms before this statement.
3. Naively, the vacuum field contains fluctuating quantum fields across all frequencies. It is not clear to me why in this
experiment the relevant vacuum fluctuations are specifically in the THz regime.

### Reviewer 2

The paper of Herter et al. “Experimentally separating vacuum fluctuations from source radiation” presents an important

various times and/or positions but also between the electric field and its conjugate quadrature in the time domain, being pi/2-
CEP-shifted electric field. By fixing the spatial separation between the probe beams, i.e. by fixing the difference in the
position in the measured correlations, and analyzing the temporal correlation behavior the authors experimentally verify
theory predictions they made in Ref. [14]. The idea of the theory proposal was that the corresponding two types of
correlations can be associated with the so-called vacuum and source contributions in the dynamics of two spatially
separated atoms coupled via the surrounded quantum electro-magnetic environment. Given that analogy, the authors
manage to show that the suggested measurements can be indeed performed. Their results quite well match the results of the
modelling of the corresponding correlations as they are captured in the two-beam EOS setup. The discussion about the role
of those vacuum and source contributions, appearing in the perturbative treatment of the dynamics of the interacting atoms
and field up to the second order, was quite important in the past. It might be somewhat outdated in the context of modern
quantum field theoretical treatments of the interaction of matter with electro-magnetic field. Nevertheless, the demonstration
that this discussion can be illuminated by an analogue measurement seems to be interesting and also highly valuable.
Thus, I would be generally in favor of publication of this paper.
Said that, I think that for giving a definitely positive recommendation the paper still lacks certain clarity and scientific rigor in
terms of the presentation and explanations. I am listing the corresponding particular issues that I noticed below:
- lines 28-29: The authors write “Beyond resolving a longstanding theoretical ambiguity, …”
This sentence looks good for the motivation but I think it contradicts to the fact that according to the current understanding
there is actually no “ambiguity” remained but rather indeed “vacuum fluctuations and source radiation can therefore be seen
as inseparable ”two sides of the same quantum mechanical coin””, as the authors also write in lines 47-48. The initial
confusions leading to the “ambiguity” seem to be rather of technical matter (ordering of the operator terms in the second
order of the perturbation theory). When the physical process is considered as a whole, there is no such issue of sorting out
the terms.
- In lines 41-43, the authors discuss the situation of two atoms. They write “On the other hand, the two atoms can exchange a
real photon.” but continue “This process, triggered by the interaction of the emitting atom with its own radiative field” jumping
in the description to a situation of just one atom. Where is then the exchange (!) of a real photon? The authors think about
one situation but seem to describe a relevant but still different another situation. That is confusing.
- In lines 43-43, the authors write “Mathematically, the individual contributions of vacuum fluctuations and source radiation
are in general not uniquely determined, since they depend on the initial ordering of two commuting operators.” Here the

can be meant, as in the paper of Dalibard, but here the description becomes so abstract that, in my opinion, it just does not
really make sense to state if some contributions are “uniquely determined” or not. Further, the explanation becomes even
more unclear with mentioning of “the initial ordering of two commuting operators”. This is a very technical description of the
things, being neither some physical phenomena, nor effects or variables, which are not even introduced in any appropriate

motivation/introductory part of the paper. Otherwise, it has to be explained clearer.
- The “operator ordering” appears again without an appropriate context in line 52.
- In line 58, “probe source radiation and vacuum field fluctuations individually for the first time” – with the use of the word

other, leading to confusion.
- Starting from line 74 the authors introduce an analogy between the version of the two-beam EOS setup
used by them in the present paper and the two-atom problem. I understand that this analogy was introduced and discussed at length in a very
thorough preceding theory paper, Ref. [14]. However, should the reader consider that paper as a kind of “Supplementary” to
the present paper? Even so, I think that the key points of the analogy should be further simplified/purified and explained in a
clear way, mentioning also the main differences in the systems and arguing why they would not be significant in the present
context. For example, a few differences: the fields considered as counterparts of atoms in the two-atom problem have a
continuous set of possible transition (photon) energies and not a discrete one. Moreover, for each transition energy many
excitations are possible and not just one, since we deal in that case with bosons. The explanations about all those things
can be organized, e.g., as a comparison table.
- The only quantities defined before showing the correlation plots in Fig. 2, are two quantities C and R in lines 76 and 76.
However, which “correlations” are then exactly plotted in Fig. 2b? Obviously, they cannot be both represented by C and R,
because R is an imaginary quantity. Moreover, R has a step in the time dependence, which is not observed in Fig. 2b. Of

check again Ref. [14]. However, I think that the measured quantities have to be precisely defined in the main text of the
manuscript, before discussing the figures and what they show. From the description stating that actually the correlations
between the electric field and the pi/2-CEP-shifted quadrature are measured, I wonder why the authors do not cite the paper
of Leitenstorfer’s group, Physical Review A 101, 033821 (2020), where such pi/2-CEP-shifted quadrature was measured (of
course, yet classically and without evaluation of the correlations). I know there is a limitation on references and there are
many citations of that group anyway but still. Moreover, I guess that the definition of the measured correlations would be
probably expressible via E and that E_(pi/2). This would, in turn, make obvious that since E_(pi/2) is the Hilbert transform of
E the same should be probably valid for the corresponding two different types of measured correlations in Fig. 2. I think this
should be made clear before discussing the consequences when interpreting the measurement in terms of the two-atom

In their work titled “Experimentally separating vacuum fluctuations from source radiation”, Alexa Herter et al report their

prediction of an experimental method of testing such correlations by means of electro-optic sampling and this present work
represent, at large, a validation of those theoretical predictions.
I find this work creative, daring, exciting and a stellar example of how experimental science should be used to lead
exploration of fundamental physics. I congratulate the authors on these heroic efforts, and I generally support the publication

criticism for authors’ consideration in the hope that it is taken as my attempt to help them to identify the weak points of the
presentation and to improve them, if possible, in order to strengthen the arguments.

1. The authors provide a compelling proposal of using EOS with QWP/HWP configurations to separate vacuum-source
contributions. I find the analogy between Fermi’s two-atom setup and the two-beam EOS sampling to be innovative and
intriguing. However, I struggle with one concept which I believe should be thoroughly clarified.

the coherent states of the two probing beams. If such, the analogy is not 1-to-1 in the sense that the two states of an atom
can only lead to sequential absorption-emission vs emission-absorption events, while the harmonic oscillator nature of the
beams can admit sequential absorption and sequential emission processes. It is possible that the two are equivalent in the
lowest order of perturbation analysis, but this should be explicated.
